1: \section{From frozen confidence to current-curvature scores}\label{sec:abstract-transport}
2: 
3: Consider a learner choosing from a finite list of available actions $\cA_t$
4: at round $t$.  After observing the context, it predicts each action's mean
5: reward $\mu_t^*(a)$ and chooses an action $a_t$ whose reward could plausibly
6: be high.  Only the chosen reward is then revealed.
7: An \emph{upper confidence bound} (UCB) makes this rule precise: its score adds
8: an uncertainty allowance to a prediction.  We call the score \emph{optimistic}
9: when it upper-bounds the true mean reward of every available action on the
10: stated confidence and certificate event.  This is a claim about mean rewards,
11: not about every noisy reward that the learner might observe.
12: 
13: \paragraph{What changes when the model is retrained?}
14: The feature vector used to interpret a past reward was fixed before that
15: reward arrived.  Keeping these collection-time vectors gives a frozen
16: reference matrix with the sequential update used by the confidence argument.
17: Recomputing the past vectors at the current model can give a different matrix,
18: even though no new rewards have been collected.  The question is how to use
19: this current matrix without silently assuming that the original confidence
20: argument still applies.
21: 
22: The prediction query $\bq_t(a)$ is the vector whose uncertainty matters for
23: action $a$; in the nonlinear specialization it is the current prediction
24: gradient.  A metric here is a symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrix: its
25: quadratic form is positive in every nonzero direction.  A query's \emph{width}
26: is its norm under the inverse metric.  It measures a geometric scale, not a
27: confidence level by itself.  Statistical confidence also needs a valid
28: nonnegative radius $\beta_t$, a prediction center $m_t(a)$, and a nonnegative
29: error allowance $b_t(a)$.  A smaller width after retraining therefore does not, by itself,
30: show that prediction error has become smaller.  A \emph{certificate} is a
31: bound that guarantees a required comparison or numerical property; measuring
32: a small discrepancy in an experiment is not itself such a guarantee.
33: 
34: \paragraph{Start with an exact current matrix and exact widths.}
35: For the moment, suppose the learner computes the current matrix and its
36: width $s_t(a)$ exactly.  Suppose also that a statistical argument bounds the
37: absolute prediction error by $\beta_t\bar s_t(a)+b_t(a)$ in the frozen matrix.
38: A valid path certificate $\bar D_t$ supplies the comparison
39: $\bar s_t(a)\le e^{\bar D_t/2}s_t(a)$ for every action.  Thus the exact-case
40: score is
41: \[
42:  U_t(a)=m_t(a)+\beta_t e^{\bar D_t/2}s_t(a)+b_t(a).
43: \]
44: On the joint confidence and certificate event, this score upper-bounds the
45: mean reward.  The multiplier enlarges the current width enough to retain
46: the supplied reference confidence.  The center must be the one justified by
47: that confidence argument; it need not be the raw nonlinear prediction.
48: \Cref{sec:corrected-center} shows how to construct it.
49: 
50: This exact case explains what transport provides: a justification for a score
51: built around current curvature.  Direct reference scoring remains an
52: alternative.  The transport argument alone establishes neither a smaller
53: uncertainty allowance nor better action choices.  The general result next
54: also allows an approximate matrix, numerical width computation, and an
55: approximately maximizing action selector.
56: 
57: \paragraph{How to read the argument.}
58: We first assume a confidence band in the frozen metric and state the
59: conditions that let a current-metric score use it.  The main result is
60: \Cref{thm:transported-ucb}; its interpretation follows the statement.
61: \Cref{sec:logarithmic-transport} then supplies geometric comparisons between
62: metrics, and \Cref{sec:corrected-center} constructs the confidence band for
63: squared loss.  \Cref{sec:closed-rates-new} combines these pieces into regret
64: rates and explains the sharper comparison available for scaled tanh.
65: The finite-action picture above is enough to follow these constructions;
66: the general protocol below also covers action spaces that cannot be listed.
67: 
68: \paragraph{The matrices and their widths.}
69: Let $\bq_t(a)\in\R^d$ be the prediction query.  We distinguish the frozen
70: reference matrix $\bVbar_t$, the exact current matrix $\bV_t$, and the SPD
71: matrix $\Calg_t$ that the algorithm actually applies.  They are also called
72: metrics because they define the norms used for uncertainty.  The reference
73: matrix has the following update, whereas the current and applied matrices
74: need not have a rank-one update:
75: \begin{align}
76:  \bVbar_1&=\lambda\bI,\nonumber\\
77:  \bVbar_{t+1}&=\bVbar_t+\sigma^{-2}\bq_t(a_t)\bq_t(a_t)^\top,
78:  \label{eq:reference-update-new}\\
79:  \bV_t&=\text{the exact current relinearized metric},\nonumber\\
80:  \Calg_t&=\text{the algorithmic SPD metric}.
81: \end{align}
82: Here $\lambda>0$ is the ridge regularization and $\sigma>0$ sets the scale
83: of the updates; it is the noise scale in the squared-loss specialization.
84: The reference update keeps each query as it was at collection time.
85: For the same current query, the matrices can give different widths:
86: \begin{equation}\label{eq:three-widths-new}
87:  \begin{aligned}
88:   \bar s_t^2(a)&=\bq_t(a)^\top\bVbar_t^{-1}\bq_t(a),\\
89:   s_t^2(a)&=\bq_t(a)^\top\bV_t^{-1}\bq_t(a),\\
90:   s_{\Calg,t}^2(a)&=\bq_t(a)^\top\Calg_t^{-1}\bq_t(a).
91:  \end{aligned}
92: \end{equation}
93: These are exact mathematical widths.  The computed upper width
94: $\hat s_t(a)$ will be a separate object, because a numerical solver need not
95: return the exact width of $\Calg_t$.
96: 
97: The frozen update also gives a way to control widths accumulated over time.
98: Its log-determinant growth, called the \emph{frozen information gain}, is
99: \begin{equation}\label{eq:frozen-gamma-new}
100:  \gamma_T
101:  :=\log\frac{\det\bVbar_{T+1}}{\det\bVbar_1}
102:  =\sum_{t=1}^T\log\!\left(1+\sigma^{-2}\bar s_t^2(a_t)\right).
103: \end{equation}
104: Each term records the contribution of the action actually chosen.  This
105: identity is why the regret proof returns to the frozen matrix even when the
106: policy scores actions using the current matrix.  Set $\gamma_0=0$, and define
107: regret as the mean reward lost relative to the best available action:
108: \begin{equation}\label{eq:regret-definition-new}
109:  \operatorname{reg}_t
110:  :=\sup_{a\in\cA_t}\mu_t^*(a)-\mu_t^*(a_t),
111:  \qquad R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\operatorname{reg}_t.
112: \end{equation}
113: 
114: \paragraph{General protocol and timing.}
115: Let $(\mathsf A,\mathcal B)$ be a standard Borel action space.  At round $t$,
116: the learner observes a context and a nonempty random action correspondence
117: $\cA_t:\Omega\to 2^{\mathsf A}$ whose graph
118: \[
119:  \operatorname{Gr}(\cA_t)
120:  :=\{(\omega,a):a\in\cA_t(\omega)\}
121:  \in\cHist_t^-\otimes\mathcal B.
122: \]
123: Here $\cHist_t^-$ is the history after the context and action correspondence
124: are observed but before fresh round-$t$ algorithmic randomization.  The variable
125: $\Omega_t$ records all round-$t$ pre-reward randomization, which may be revealed
126: in sequential stages, and $\cHist_t=\cHist_t^-\vee\sigma(\Omega_t)$ contains
127: that randomization but not the reward.  The restrictions to
128: $\operatorname{Gr}(\cA_t)$ of
129: $(\omega,a)\mapsto\mu_t^*(a),\bq_t(a),m_t(a),b_t(a),\hat s_t(a)$, and, once
130: defined below, $U_t(a)$ are assumed jointly measurable with respect to
131: $\cHist_t\otimes\mathcal B$.  We also assume explicitly that
132: $\sup_{a\in\cA_t}\mu_t^*(a)$ and $\sup_{a\in\cA_t}U_t(a)$ are finite
133: $\cHist_t$-measurable random variables, that the oracle below returns a $\cHist_t$-measurable
134: selector in $\cA_t$, and that the simultaneous confidence and all certificate
135: events below, including path, operator, all-domain solver-upper, and
136: played-action sharpness validity, are measurable.  These are
137: substantive assumptions; standard-Borel structure
138: and graph measurability alone do not make every supremum or selector measurable.
139: 
140: The reference metric $\bVbar_t$ and, when used, the representation parameter
141: $\btheta_t$ are determined from the prefix history and are
142: $\cHist_t^-$-measurable.  The exact current metric $\bV_t$ is likewise formed
143: before the fresh certificate randomization and is $\cHist_t^-$-measurable.  The realized algorithmic operator
144: $\Calg_t$, path envelope $\bar D_t$, condition factors
145: $\kappa_{-,t},\kappa_{+,t}$, solver-width map $\hat s_t(\cdot)$, sharpness
146: factor $\alpha_t$, oracle tolerance $\xi_t$, and selected action $a_t$ may
147: depend on $\Omega_t$ and are required only to be $\cHist_t$-measurable.  Thus
148: ``predictable'' below is reserved for $\cHist_t^-$-measurable quantities;
149: quantities that may use $\Omega_t$ are called pre-reward measurable.  The
150: reward is observed only after $a_t$ is selected.
151: 
152: \paragraph{What must be certified.}
153: The next assumption separates statistical confidence from the comparisons
154: needed to use it.  The confidence band concerns the center $m_t(a)$ and the
155: frozen width.  The path and operator certificates compare matrices.  The
156: solver certificate controls the width that enters the score.
157: Its quantifiers have different jobs: an upper-valid width is needed for every
158: scored action to preserve optimism, while an upper bound on excess width
159: (``sharpness'') is needed only for the action played to control regret.
160: All of these objects must be available before that action's reward is seen.
161: 
162: \begin{assumption}[Reference confidence and operational certificates]
163: \label{asm:abstract-transport}
164: For predictable $\beta_t\ge0$ and pre-reward measurable center $m_t(a)$ and
165: action-dependent envelope $b_t(a)\ge0$, a measurable simultaneous confidence
166: event satisfies
167: \begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-confidence-new}
168:  |\mu_t^*(a)-m_t(a)|\le\beta_t\bar s_t(a)+b_t(a)
169:  \qquad\text{for every }a\in\cA_t.
170: \end{equation}
171: There is an absolutely continuous SPD path $\bV_t(\tau)$ from
172: $\bVbar_t$ to $\bV_t$ with a pre-reward certificate
173: \begin{equation}\label{eq:path-length-new}
174:  \begin{aligned}
175:   \mathcal D_t
176:   &:=\int_0^1\!\left\|
177:   \bV_t(\tau)^{-1/2}\dot\bV_t(\tau)\bV_t(\tau)^{-1/2}
178:   \right\|_{\rm op}d\tau\\
179:   &\le\bar D_t<\infty.
180:  \end{aligned}
181: \end{equation}
182: The algorithmic operator has a pre-reward two-sided certificate
183: \begin{equation}\label{eq:operator-sandwich-new}
184:  0<\kappa_{-,t}\le\kappa_{+,t}<\infty,\qquad
185:  \kappa_{-,t}\bV_t\preceq\Calg_t\preceq\kappa_{+,t}\bV_t.
186: \end{equation}
187: Finally, the solver returns a jointly measurable pre-reward width map
188: $\hat s_t(a)\ge0$ such that, on a measurable solver event,
189: \begin{equation}\label{eq:solver-interface-new}
190:  \begin{aligned}
191:   s_{\Calg,t}(a)&\le\hat s_t(a)
192:   &&\text{for every }a\in\cA_t,\\
193:   \hat s_t(a_t)&\le\alpha_t s_{\Calg,t}(a_t),
194:   &&\alpha_t\ge1.
195:  \end{aligned}
196: \end{equation}
197: The first condition is an all-domain optimism certificate.  The second is
198: required only at the played action.
199: \end{assumption}
200: 
201: The general score combines the center, the converted uncertainty allowance,
202: and the current error allowance.  The operator factor accounts for using
203: $\Calg_t$ in place of $\bV_t$, and $\hat s_t(a)$ is the width actually used
204: by the selector:
205: \begin{equation}\label{eq:transported-score-new}
206:  U_t(a)=m_t(a)
207:  +\beta_t e^{\bar D_t/2}\sqrt{\kappa_{+,t}}\,\hat s_t(a)
208:  +b_t(a),
209: \end{equation}
210: Let a pre-reward oracle return a $\cHist_t$-measurable selector
211: $a_t\in\cA_t$ satisfying
212: \begin{equation}\label{eq:approx-score-oracle-new}
213:  U_t(a_t)\ge\sup_{a\in\cA_t}U_t(a)-\xi_t,\qquad \xi_t\ge0.
214: \end{equation}
215: The tolerance $\xi_t$ measures how far the selected score may fall below the
216: best score; it is not a condition on nonlinear model training.  Regret is
217: defined against the mean-reward supremum, so an optimal action need not exist.
218: 
219: \begin{remark}[One realized solver-width map]
220: The all-domain solver upper condition, the played-action sharpness condition,
221: and the approximate-score-oracle inequality refer to the same realized width
222: map $\hat s_t(\cdot)$.  Refining the selected action's solve after selection
223: must not silently replace the value used in $U_t(a_t)$.  If refinement changes
224: $\hat s_t(a_t)$, the oracle inequality must be checked again, or the original
225: score width must remain the theorem object.  Any randomized post-selection
226: verification needs its own pre-draw filtration and conditional failure
227: allocation.  No all-action sharpness condition is required.
228: \end{remark}

252: \paragraph{The regret guarantee.}
253: Under these conditions, optimism bounds the loss at the selected action by
254: its uncertainty and bias terms.  Comparing that selected width back to the
255: reference width lets the frozen information gain control their accumulation.
256: The theorem states this conclusion on the joint event where the supplied
257: confidence and certificates hold.
258: 
259: \begin{theorem}[Estimator- and solver-agnostic confidence transport]
260: \label{thm:transported-ucb}
261: Under the protocol above with $\lambda>0$ and $\sigma>0$, suppose
262: \Cref{asm:abstract-transport} holds, the score obeys
263: \eqref{eq:transported-score-new}--\eqref{eq:approx-score-oracle-new}, and
264: $\|\bq_t(a)\|_2\le G$.  On the joint confidence and certificate event, the
265: instantaneous regret satisfies
266: \begin{equation}\label{eq:instantaneous-transport-new}
267:  \operatorname{reg}_t\le
268:  \beta_t\!\left[1+\alpha_t e^{\bar D_t}
269:  \sqrt{\frac{\kappa_{+,t}}{\kappa_{-,t}}}\right]\bar s_t(a_t)
270:  +2b_t(a_t)+\xi_t.
271: \end{equation}
272: Consequently,
273: \begin{align}
274: R_T
275: &\le
276: \sqrt{\left(\sigma^2+\frac{G^2}{\lambda}\right)\gamma_T
277: \sum_{t=1}^T\beta_t^2
278: \left[1+\alpha_t e^{\bar D_t}
279: \sqrt{\frac{\kappa_{+,t}}{\kappa_{-,t}}}\right]^2}
280: \nonumber\\[-1mm]
281: &\quad+2\sum_{t=1}^Tb_t(a_t)+\sum_{t=1}^T\xi_t.\label{eq:sharp-transport-regret-new}
282: \end{align}
283: In particular, the simpler bound
284: \begin{align}
285: R_T
286: &\le2\sqrt{\left(\sigma^2+\frac{G^2}{\lambda}\right)\gamma_T
287: \sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t^2\beta_t^2e^{2\bar D_t}
288: \frac{\kappa_{+,t}}{\kappa_{-,t}}}
289: \nonumber\\[-1mm]
290: &\quad+2\sum_{t=1}^Tb_t(a_t)+\sum_{t=1}^T\xi_t
291: \label{eq:simple-transport-regret-new}
292: \end{align}
293: holds.  The bias envelope enters twice and the approximate-oracle error enters
294: once.  If the confidence event has probability at least $1-\delta$ and the
295: joint certificate event has probability at least $1-\delta_{\rm cert}$, these
296: bounds hold with probability at least $1-\delta-\delta_{\rm cert}$.
297: \end{theorem}
298: 
299: \paragraph{Reading the bound.}
300: The instantaneous bound has a statistical radius $\beta_t$, a frozen width
301: $\bar s_t(a_t)$, and a factor accounting for transport and computation.
302: The exponential $e^{\bar D_t}$ reflects two comparisons: a factor
303: $e^{\bar D_t/2}$ makes the current-width score optimistic, and another
304: compares the selected current width back to the frozen width for the regret
305: proof.  The ratio $\kappa_{+,t}/\kappa_{-,t}$ accounts for operator distortion,
306: and $\alpha_t$ accounts for excess width from the solver.  The additive terms
307: charge current bias and approximate score maximization.
308: 
309: Validity does not ensure that this bound is informative.  A large path
310: envelope, a weak lower operator bound, a loose solver width, or persistent
311: bias can make it vacuous.  In particular, an upper operator comparison alone
312: can support the outward comparison but cannot supply the return comparison
313: used by the displayed regret bound.
314: 
315: \paragraph{Why keep direct reference scoring as a comparator?}
316: Once a reference-confidence band is available, the learner can score actions
317: with its reference widths directly.  The next proposition states that
318: policy's guarantee on its own selected history.  It provides a baseline for
319: understanding the additional factors required by transport.
320: 
321: \begin{proposition}[Frozen-width UCB on its own trajectory]
322: \label{prop:frozen-width-ucb}
323: Keep the timing, measurability, bounded-query, and frozen-update assumptions
324: above, and assume \eqref{eq:abstract-confidence-new} along the trajectory of
325: the policy that uses
326: \[
327:  U_t^{\rm fr}(a)=m_t(a)+\beta_t\bar s_t(a)+b_t(a).
328: \]
329: Assume its score supremum is finite and measurable and its pre-reward
330: measurable selector satisfies
331: $U_t^{\rm fr}(a_t)\ge\sup_{a\in\cA_t}U_t^{\rm fr}(a)-\xi_t$.
332: On the reference-confidence event,
333: \begin{align}
334:  \operatorname{reg}_t
335:  &\le 2\beta_t\bar s_t(a_t)+2b_t(a_t)+\xi_t,\nonumber\\
336:  R_T
337:  &\le 2\sqrt{\left(\sigma^2+\frac{G^2}{\lambda}\right)
338:  \gamma_T\sum_{t=1}^T\beta_t^2}
339:  +2\sum_{t=1}^Tb_t(a_t)+\sum_{t=1}^T\xi_t.
340:  \label{eq:frozen-width-regret}
341: \end{align}
342: All quantities are evaluated on this policy's own selected history.  No path,
343: current-metric, or operator certificate is needed for this score.  If its
344: reference-confidence event has probability at least $1-\delta$, so does this
345: guarantee.
346: \end{proposition}
347: 
348: Holding the history fixed gives a different comparison.  If the confidence
349: band is the only information supplied about the mean, reducing its upper
350: endpoint would exclude a mean that the band still allows.  Transport cannot
351: justify that reduction merely by expressing the same information in another
352: matrix.  This is a statement about widths on the same history, not about the
353: regret of policies that collect different histories.
354: 
355: \begin{proposition}[Reference-width floor on a fixed history]
356: \label{prop:reference-width-floor}
357: On the certificate event of \Cref{asm:abstract-transport}, every scored action
358: satisfies
359: \begin{equation}\label{eq:reference-width-floor}
360:  w_t^{\rm tr}(a):=e^{\bar D_t/2}\sqrt{\kappa_{+,t}}\hat s_t(a)
361:  \ge \bar s_t(a).
362: \end{equation}
363: For exact current widths, the actionwise multiplier
364: \begin{equation}\label{eq:actionwise-width-ratio}
365:  c_t(a)=\begin{cases}
366:  \bar s_t(a)/s_t(a),&\bq_t(a)\ne0,\\
367:  1,&\bq_t(a)=0
368:  \end{cases}
369:  \qquad\text{satisfies}\qquad c_t(a)s_t(a)=\bar s_t(a).
370: \end{equation}
371: Thus this exact actionwise correction reproduces the frozen-width score when
372: the center, radius, and bias are the same.
373: 
374: More generally, fix an action and $m_t(a)$, $b_t(a)$, $\beta_t>0$, and
375: $\bar s_t(a)$.  If the only restriction on its mean is the full interval
376: \eqref{eq:abstract-confidence-new}, a score
377: $m_t(a)+\beta_t w_t(a)+b_t(a)$ is an upper bound for every mean in that
378: interval if and only if $w_t(a)\ge\bar s_t(a)$.
379: \end{proposition}
380: 
381: The last statement concerns the uncertainty set supplied by one confidence
382: band.  Additional restrictions on the mean, a different center, or another
383: simultaneous confidence event can change that set.  An exact scalar endpoint
384: distance supplies a worst-direction multiplier, not necessarily the
385: actionwise equality in \eqref{eq:actionwise-width-ratio}.  These are
386: same-history comparisons; they do not order the realized regret of policies
387: whose actions and subsequent histories differ.
388: Evaluating the ratio in \eqref{eq:actionwise-width-ratio} as written uses the
389: reference width itself and supplies no computational shortcut.  This
390: observation is not a general computational lower bound.
391: 
392: \begin{remark}[The reference band alone does not justify a smaller width]
393: \label{rem:naive-width-band-counterexample}
394: Consider an abstract confidence-band instance with $D>0$,
395: $\bVbar=\bI_2$, $\bV=\operatorname{diag}(e^D,e^{-D})$, and
396: $\bq=(1,0)^\top$.  Take $m=b=0$, $\beta>0$, and $\mu^*=\beta$.
397: Then $\bar s=1$ and $s=e^{-D/2}$, so
398: \[
399:  |\mu^*-m|=\beta\bar s+b,\qquad
400:  m+\beta s+b=\beta e^{-D/2}<\mu^*.
